title: After 18-year-old’s online exploitation and death, mom wonders why police didn’t search devices right away

image.caption: A mother in Newfoundland is fighting for justice for her teen who died by suicide in April after years of being exploited online. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC)

blocks.text: WARNING: This story contains references to suicide, abuse and graphic material that may be upsetting to some readers.

A grieving mother in St. John's says she and her family were left to find their own evidence after police didn't investigate signs her teen was being exploited by a sadistic online network, despite RCMP in the province being the first police force in Canada to warn parents about the threat more than two years ago.

The family — who CBC News is not identifying for fear of retaliation by online predators — reached out to the fifth estate earlier this year after seeing the program's investigative documentary about 764 — an online network of violent extremists that targets vulnerable minors. It also tries to coerce them into sending sexually explicit messages and images, doing self-harm — including carving their predators' names into their skin as a sign of devotion — and even killing themselves.
The mother says her teen, who we are referring to by the initial J, was being exploited in a similar manner and died by suicide in April at the age of 18.
J was an 18-year-old in Newfoundland who loved sunrises, sunsets, their family and their dog. They died by suicide in April. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Since their death, J's mother says she has been left to scour her child's devices and journals and has found evidence of multiple usernames exploiting her child, utilizing similar tactics used by members of 764, including sexual exploitation and pressure to self-harm.
While police were aware of J's victimization after J attempted suicide in June 2025, J's mother says police did not take J's devices for analysis then or after J died by suicide this past April.
Mom says police ‘asked for nothing’ after teen’s death, online exploitation

Following an interview with the fifth estate, Sgt. Brent Perry, who runs the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary's integrated internet child exploitation unit, reached out to J's mother. He apologized for not "properly" communicating the force's "offer/ability to further this investigation" and has since taken the devices for review.
An inner world of exploitation
J's mother is speaking out now, she says, to find justice for J.
"I feel like this is my role now as J's mom … so the world can see what happens online because a lot of us are blinded to it and J's not here to tell the story themselves."
J left behind multiple phones and journals for their family in which they outline the extent of their online exploitation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

J's vulnerability can be seen in journal entries, drawings and videos they left behind. In one recording, when J was 15, J speaks about their struggles with mental health, suicidal ideation and self-harm.
J's journal entries also reveal a window into a sadistic online world where J's vulnerability left them targeted and trapped.

According to their mother, J — who loved sunrises, their family and their dog deeply — was struggling with their gender identity during the pandemic and began to spend more time isolated in their room on their phone.

It was only after a suicide attempt in June 2025 that J ended up in hospital and disclosed they had been exploited online by several individuals who had pushed them to record and share images of them self-harming and attempting suicide.
J's mother said she was shocked by what her child shared.
"J explicitly said: ‘They told me to do this, they told to kill myself, they told me to cut myself. They told me, you know, they made me do it. I had no choice. They knew where we lived.'"
For what would have been J's 19th birthday in August, the family placed a purple bench in memory of the teen, at a spot where they enjoyed watching the sunset. (Submitted by J's family)

J's mom called Canada's national tipline, Cybertip.ca, which alerted police. An officer from the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary's integrated internet child exploitation unit came to the hospital and interviewed J.
But according to their mother, a few months later, an officer informed the family that without more information, the investigation was stalled.
Previous police warning

Just a year before, Newfoundland and Labrador RCMP was the first police department in Canada to warn the public about violent online networks that went by names like 764 or CVLT — groups targeting vulnerable children as young as eight on popular social media, gaming and streaming platforms.

At the time, police warned caregivers about how members of the group often invite minors to private chatrooms where they sexually exploit and groom them — for the main purpose of gaining clout within the group.
Since that advisory, the unit has been investigating at least half a dozen cases in the last year. In June, the unit held a news conference to alert the public of another 764 victim in the province.

items: RNC warns parents after youth targeted by extortion group through Roblox

blocks.text: Despite the growing awareness, and J's case bearing the hallmarks of 764's exploitation, J's mother says her child's online abuse was not flagged as another potential case.
J's mother says she can't understand why her child's case wasn't examined more closely given the RCMP had issued the 764 alert just a year before police became aware of J's exploitation.

"When it came to the 764 and knowing that my child was only a year after that and nothing was done — like it was basically dismissed and said: ‘This is it, there's nothing we can do….' Like, why didn't they take this more seriously? Why didn't they ask to see [the] devices?"
Instead, the family says after J's death, an officer told them to reach out if they found any evidence themselves.
J had several devices and in a note left behind included passwords and pointed to where the family could find phones, computers and journals documenting the abuse they endured.

With the help of family members, J's mother spent weeks poring through J's journals, combing through accounts and chats as well as images and videos and found evidence of multiple individuals exploiting her child.
"Why do I, as a parent who just lost my child, have to go through all of this looking for that explicit content? You know, like it's, to me that's torture."
J's mother has kept a number of J's personal belongings close, including the teen's baby blanket. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC)

When asked why a family in that situation would be left to gather evidence of their dead child's exploitation, Perry said he could not speak about individual cases. But he acknowledged his empathy for the family.
"I'm a father myself and that issue is very much alive to me," Perry told the fifth estate.
"I'll reiterate that if a family has information that they believe would be of interest to the police to investigate, our door is always open to investigate and hear what information they have."
764 offshoots continue to evolve

Understanding how to tackle the larger problem of 764 and its offshoots is still in its infancy, says Marc-André Argentino, an extremism expert with Public Safety Canada who has been tracking 764 and affiliate groups since 2022.
Argentino says 764 and its offshoots continue to evolve from a loose network urging minors to self-harm to pressuring members to commit acts of public violence.
"This is not fictitious. And it is as bad as we are saying. And actually it is worse."
764 and its related groups draw inspiration from a satanic neo-Nazi movement called the Order of Nine Angles (O9A). (CBC)
Argentino has spent much of his time in the last year training thousands of front-line workers around the world, including 2,000 police officers in Canada, to recognize signs of 764.

"We have a challenge talking about 764 and the network simply because of the type of harms and criminal acts that are perpetrated, the extreme nature of these acts," he said, adding that the fact youths are often behind the violence is hard for many to comprehend.
As the threat escalated, Canada was the first country in the world to designate 764 a terrorist threat in December 2025.

items: Canada becomes 1st country to list extremist network 764 as terrorists

blocks.text: Since then, police have made multiple 764-related arrests across the country, including in Quebec City, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan, as well as identifying several victims in British Columbia.
In an email, a spokesperson for the RCMP said while it cannot share how many 764 cases are being investigated, the "threat is evolving and increasingly involves young people."
Calls for legislation

At a recent event in Ottawa, parents, young people and advocacy groups called on the federal government to implement its online harms legislation, the Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34), which was tabled in June 2026.

The bill is designed to implement age-appropriate protections and safeguards for younger users, including safer design features and measures to reduce children's exposure to harmful material and high-risk online interactions. The bill is expected to become law next year.
J's mother says the legislation can't come soon enough.
She has spent hours going down dark online corners hoping to hold someone accountable and find justice for her child.
Police apologize, take devices
In the email to J's mother that was sent a day after the fifth estate interviewed Perry, he offered to support her analysis of J's devices "to further her search for answers."
Sgt. Brent Perry is in charge of the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary’s integrated internet child exploitation unit. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Perry added that "it has recently come to my attention that our offer/ability to further this investigation was not communicated properly and for that I offer my sincere apology."

The email, sent in June, was the first significant development since J's death in April. In that time, J's mother had found evidence to share, including images of who J claimed was their main predator and messages offering money in exchange for J to carve a name into J's skin.
The RCMP has since asked J's mother to bring in everything she found — including J's devices.
"I provided whatever information I possibly could," she said.
Her voice breaking, she added that she could feel J working through her "to keep me going, to push further and to keep searching. I so badly want justice."
Police have since copied most of the devices and told her the investigation could take months.
